title: Notion Custom Agents: What the Credit Pricing Means for Your Team
content:
Screenshot of notion.com (source)

Notion's Custom Agents are described on Notion's pricing page as AI agents that "handle repetitive tasks autonomously." The technology works as described, but it runs on a metered credit system, so agents that run constantly in the background cost more than occasional ones. Whether that overhead is worth it depends on how often an agent runs and how much work each run replaces. Notion's own examples put typical per-run costs at roughly $0.03 to $0.30, so do the math before scaling.

Here are the mechanics, based on Notion's pricing and help pages (linked at the end). This post is analysis of that documentation, not a hands-on test.

What's Actually Going On

Screenshot of notion.com (source)

Custom Agents are a metered product bolted onto a per-seat plan

Notion's own pricing page lists Custom Agents as "AI agents handle repetitive tasks autonomously, so your team doesn't have to," free to try, then $10 per 1,000 credits . This is easy to miss: it is not "included in your plan." It's a consumption product layered on top of seats you're already paying for.

The credit math varies with what the agent does. Custom Agents spend credits every time they run a task, more complex tasks use more, and credits are shared across the workspace, so every agent draws from the same balance regardless of who built it - with usage rising when agents read more content, take more actions, or run more often . Notion is upfront that reading longer pages or scanning larger databases costs more, multi-step workflows cost more, frequently triggered agents cost more over time, and advanced models cost more .

Notion even publishes a worked example: an agent similar to a "Status update agent" running 60 times a month works out to roughly $4.80–$10.80 per month . That's one agent doing one narrow job, with a spread of more than 2x on the estimate.

When you run out, the agents just stop

This is a detail worth checking before you buy. If your workspace doesn't have enough credits, Custom Agents pause automatically until credits reset or an admin adds more - and premium models pause too . Admins get in-app and email notifications at 80% and 100% of credit usage .

So the system has a documented failure mode: agents pause when credits run out. Notion's mitigation is alerts to admins at 80% and 100% of credit usage, so someone has to be watching them.

There are two separate meters, and one of them isn't the one you think

Notion runs a general AI usage allowance and a credit system, and they don't overlap. The usage allowance covers things like your personal Notion Agent, image generation, and page translation - it doesn't apply to Custom Agents or Workers, which use credits instead, and it doesn't cover certain premium models, which also spend credits . Separately, AI Meeting Notes carries its own 10-hour daily cap . And when the allowance runs out, some AI features pause until it refreshes, which happens within six hours .

Workers - the code layer - are cheaper per unit: Notion says Workers typically cost $0.0023 per run, about 4,348 runs per 1,000 credits , and Workers use micro credits because they run predictable, repeatable code, while Custom Agents usually use more because they rely on AI to reason through next steps .

Notion has built a whole governance layer for spend

Notion provides admin tooling for cost control. Admins can choose who can create agents, set per-agent credit limits, and - on Enterprise - set a workspace-level credit limit applying to all new and existing agents, all from the usage dashboard . Notion's own admin guidance tells you to factor in frequency rather than just complexity, because a simple agent running hourly can cost more than a complex one running weekly, and to review the dashboard monthly at first .

My Take

Screenshot of notion.com (source)

The marketing frames Custom Agents as removing work. Because they bill by usage, adopting them also adds a task: monitoring credit spend. Whether that is worth it depends on how much work each run replaces.

Here is the core concern: the pricing is variable. The pricing model scales with frequency and depth: agents that run on a schedule or trigger frequently use more credits over time, so a frequently triggered agent costs more than an occasional one. That makes run frequency a cost decision, though per-agent credit limits and a usage dashboard are available to manage it.

Second, pausing is a reliability consideration. If a weekly client status roll-up pauses because another agent used the shared credit pool, the process becomes unreliable unless someone is watching the 80% and 100% alerts or has set per-agent limits. Pausing is documented behavior, so plan for it.

A useful question is unit economics: what does this task cost per run, how many runs per month, and is that number smaller than the value of my time? Notion deserves credit for publishing enough detail to do that math.

Teams already running agents may have an owner for the credit dashboard and high-volume, repetitive work, which fits a usage-based model. This post has no data on how many teams that describes.

The Counterpoint

Screenshot of notion.com (source)

The strongest argument against this view: metered pricing is a straightforward way to pay for what you use, rather than a flat seat fee. Notion gives you real levers: per-agent credit limits, an Auto model setting that matches the model to the task, and cheap Workers for deterministic jobs. Notion's published examples start at a few cents per run, so a low-volume agent can cost only a few dollars a month.

That's fair, and this post isn't calling it a scam. But a product that requires a spend-governance practice carries real overhead: Notion's own guidance is to review the dashboard monthly at first.

Bottom Line

If you're a solo user or a small team, consider whether Notion's included AI for search and drafting, plus deterministic automation (a Worker, a scheduled sync, or plain templates), covers your needs before paying for Custom Agents.

If you're 25+ people with genuinely high-volume repetitive work, do this before you buy: pick one agent, run it through the free trial period, read the credits dashboard, multiply cost-per-run by realistic monthly runs, and set a per-agent limit on day one. If the number isn't obviously less than the labor it replaces, don't scale it.

FAQ

Are Notion's Custom Agents included in the Business plan? No. Notion's pricing page lists them as free to try, then $10 per 1,000 credits , on top of your seats. The general AI usage allowance doesn't cover Custom Agents or Workers .

What happens if my workspace runs out of credits?

Custom Agents pause automatically until credits reset or an admin adds more, and premium models pause too.

You'll get notified at 80% and 100% usage.

Are Workers cheaper than agents? Yes. Notion puts Workers at roughly $0.0023 per run - about 4,348 runs per 1,000 credits , because they run predictable, repeatable code rather than AI reasoning .

Is any of this a reason to leave Notion? This post covers one feature, not the platform. Notion's core workspace is unaffected; just don't budget for agents as if they were included.

Correction note (October 2026): replaced an invented marketing quote with Notion's actual wording, removed unsupported claims about "the vast majority of small teams" and "silent" failures (Notion alerts admins at 80% and 100%), and softened intent and incentive claims. Sources: Notion pricing, Custom Agents pricing help, Notion AI usage allowance, Workers pricing.
